ev-optimal-control-problem-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 explicitly frames AA203 as a breadth-first course over the main techniques in optimal control and learning-based control. The timestamp supports the site's course-level claim that optimal control and learning-based control are the two organizing poles of the playlist.
ev-optimal-control-problem-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The site turns this syllabus framing into the broader learner thesis that action choice, dynamics, cost, constraints, and learning form one connected control problem.

ev-state-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 uses a drone/car example to say that a sensor gives information about the state of the system, including environmental observation and speed. This supports the concept page's claim that state is the information carried forward for control.
ev-state-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page generalizes from the lecture's sensor/state example to the broader criterion: the state should contain what the dynamics and decision rule need for the next action.

ev-dynamics-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 explains that control requires modeling the system and gives the shower-temperature example as a thermodynamic model of how water affects heat. This supports treating dynamics as the rule connecting action, system behavior, and future state.
ev-dynamics-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page expands the example into the general control-language role of dynamics: propagating the consequence of an action through time.

ev-objective-cost-function-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 links stability with an objective of tracking a reference signal, using thermostat temperature tracking as the example. This supports the idea that objectives score what controlled behavior should do.
ev-objective-cost-function-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page translates tracking into the broader cost-function language of comparing futures by safety, effort, error, and task success.

ev-value-function-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 10 reviews the Bellman equation in an infinite-horizon MDP setting and names the optimal value function as the object being computed, with reward replacing cost in the influence/reinforcement-learning framing.
ev-value-function-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page explains why this object matters for decision making: it stores future consequence in a number attached to a state.

ev-bellman-recursion-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 7 says dynamic-programming recursion is carried out for each possible state value and can produce a globally optimal solution under the discretized state setup. This supports the Bellman page's state-indexed recursion framing.
ev-bellman-recursion-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page recasts that mathematical recursion as now-plus-future accounting so a learner can recognize Bellman structure in new control problems.

ev-model-predictive-control-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 11 announces the transition into model predictive control after reachability and links it to continuous-time closed-loop optimal control. This supports the site treating MPC as optimization embedded in a feedback loop.
ev-model-predictive-control-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page supplies the standard receding-horizon operation, which is consistent with the lecture topic but goes beyond the short timestamp's introductory wording.

ev-recursive-feasibility-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 12 identifies persistent feasibility as a key property for an MPC pipeline and then introduces stability as another desired property. This directly supports the recursive-feasibility and stability-under-replanning pages.
ev-recursive-feasibility-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page sharpens 'persistent feasibility' into the learner test that today's MPC action must leave tomorrow's optimization problem solvable.

ev-imitation-learning-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 15 distinguishes the learning-based-control block from classical methods and names imitation learning and reinforcement learning as the two subfamilies being organized for the learner.
ev-imitation-learning-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the practical interpretation that demonstrations can stand in for a reward or dynamics model that the designer cannot write cleanly.

ev-reinforcement-learning-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 16 contrasts imitation learning from demonstrations with inverse reinforcement learning and the reward/objective behind expert behavior. This supports the site connection among demonstration learning, reward, policy, and RL framing.
ev-reinforcement-learning-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page generalizes the lecture contrast into the broader RL idea of learning behavior from interaction, reward, and delayed consequences.

ev-policy-optimization-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 18 explicitly introduces policy optimization as the second main model-free reinforcement-learning family and contrasts it with value-based methods where the policy is implicit in the value function.
ev-policy-optimization-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page turns that contrast into the first-principles explanation that policy optimization adjusts the decision rule directly.

ev-model-based-rl-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 19 closes the course roadmap by moving from model-free policy optimization to model-based RL. The timestamp supports the site's placement of model-based RL as the final learning-based-control family.
ev-model-based-rl-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page expands the roadmap transition into the method idea that learned or known models can support planning and reduce real trial-and-error.

ev-action-control-input-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 introduces AA203 as optimal and learning-based control and situates the instructor's work in robot autonomy. This supports using control input/action as part of the course's basic control vocabulary, though the timestamp is introductory rather than a detailed actuator example.
ev-action-control-input-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The concept page supplies the more precise first-principles distinction between a desired outcome and the command a controller can actually issue.

ev-horizon-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 1 introduces final time of operation in a double-integrator example. This supports the horizon concept as the time span over which the control problem is defined.
ev-horizon-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page generalizes final time into the learner-facing question of how far ahead the controller must reason before delayed consequences matter.

ev-constraints-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 2 distinguishes an open set from constraints and gives a bounded interval as an example with lower and upper bounds. This supports the constraint page's claim that constraints restrict the feasible decision set.
ev-constraints-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page translates finite-dimensional constraint language into control settings where physical, safety, and actuator limits bound the trajectory.

ev-feasibility-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 12 states that the MPC loop should have a feasible solution at each point in time. This directly supports the feasibility page and overlaps with recursive feasibility in the MPC block.
ev-feasibility-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page makes explicit the diagnostic order: before asking what is optimal, a controller must know whether any legal trajectory remains.

ev-static-optimization-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 2 says the class will review key concepts behind classical nonlinear optimization over finitely many decision variables because those insights support optimal and learning-based control. This supports static optimization as a foundational component rather than the whole course.
ev-static-optimization-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page draws the boundary between snapshot optimization and time-coupled control problems.

ev-gradient-first-order-condition-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 2 explains differentiability through a first-order approximation using the gradient and a small displacement. This supports the concept page's local-improvement interpretation of gradients and first-order conditions.
ev-gradient-first-order-condition-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page connects the local calculus statement to the control learner's practical question: which tiny decision change improves the objective?

ev-calculus-of-variations-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 3 states the optimal-control problem as finding an admissible control that causes a differential-equation system to follow an admissible trajectory minimizing a functional. This directly supports the calculus-of-variations page.
ev-calculus-of-variations-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page expands the lecture's formal statement into the idea that the unknown is a whole path, not an isolated scalar decision.

ev-costate-adjoint-variable-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 4 connects constrained finite-dimensional optimization, Lagrange multipliers, and the move of adding constraints to the objective. This supports the costate page's analogy between multipliers and trajectory-level shadow prices.
ev-costate-adjoint-variable-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page uses that analogy to explain costates as backward prices on state deviations through future dynamics.

ev-hamiltonian-optimal-control-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 4 defines the Hamiltonian as augmenting the cost with the constraint through costate variables and uses it to state optimality conditions. This directly supports the Hamiltonian concept page.
ev-hamiltonian-optimal-control-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page turns the formal optimality condition into the plain-language role of pricing immediate cost together with future state sensitivity.

ev-indirect-methods-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 4 locates indirect methods in the open-loop optimal-control roadmap and contrasts the upcoming move to direct methods. This supports the method-family boundary between deriving optimality conditions and transcribing the problem directly.
ev-indirect-methods-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page explains the operational meaning of indirect methods: derive necessary equations first, then solve the resulting boundary-value structure.

ev-direct-transcription-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 6 announces the shift from indirect methods to direct methods as another class of open-loop control strategies. This supports the direct-methods entry point, though the timestamp itself is introductory.
ev-direct-transcription-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The direct-transcription page supplies the detailed discretization interpretation and should eventually be paired with a later timestamp that names transcription more explicitly.

ev-shooting-methods-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 6 explains that control parameterization methods are also known as shooting and that they discretize time while parameterizing controls. This directly supports the shooting-methods page.
ev-shooting-methods-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the learner-facing picture of guessing controls, simulating forward, and adjusting the guess until endpoint and cost conditions are acceptable.

ev-collocation-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 6 distinguishes state-and-control parameterization methods, also known as collocation methods, from control-parameterization/shooting methods. This supports the collocation page's method classification.
ev-collocation-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page explains the implication of that classification: the path and dynamics are enforced at selected grid or collocation points.

ev-trajectory-optimization-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 6 discusses deploying a nominal path with a closed-loop module that tracks the plan and steers back toward it when reality deviates. This supports the site distinction between planned trajectory and feedback tracking.
ev-trajectory-optimization-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page generalizes the discussion into trajectory optimization as choosing the planned path under dynamics and constraints before execution.

ev-dynamic-programming-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 7 introduces dynamic programming as a procedural way to solve for optimal closed-loop control policies and immediately notes its computational intensity. This directly supports the dynamic-programming page.
ev-dynamic-programming-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page turns that course framing into the concept of solving state-indexed future-cost subproblems rather than enumerating full action sequences.

ev-stochastic-dynamic-programming-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 9 introduces disturbances modeled as random variables with an assumed probability distribution. This supports stochastic dynamic programming as dynamic programming under uncertain next-state outcomes.
ev-stochastic-dynamic-programming-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the Bellman interpretation: expected future value replaces a single deterministic next-state value.

ev-lqr-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 8 presents LQR as an example that applies dynamic-programming recursion and is also a control problem of interest in its own right. This directly supports the LQR concept page.
ev-lqr-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page expands the timestamp into the LQR mechanism: local linear and quadratic structure gives tractable feedback for small deviations.

ev-local-quadratic-approximation-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 8 states the assumption of a quadratic cost with terminal, state, and control penalties. This supports the local-quadratic-approximation page's claim that quadratic structure is a local replacement for a harder nonlinear shape.
ev-local-quadratic-approximation-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the boundary condition that local quadratic reasoning is credible only near the operating region where the approximation remains accurate.

ev-stability-under-replanning-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 12 says the MPC discussion will move from persistent feasibility to stability, and frames both as properties to imbue in the MPC control pipeline. This supports the stability-under-replanning page.
ev-stability-under-replanning-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page explains why repeated feasible optimization is not enough: replanning also needs a condition that creates long-run progress rather than cycling or drift.

ev-behavioral-cloning-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 15 describes behavior cloning as supervised learning of behavior and connects it to learning a parametric mapping from inputs to outputs. This directly supports the behavioral-cloning page.
ev-behavioral-cloning-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the control-specific closed-loop caveat: supervised action accuracy does not by itself guarantee recovery after the learned policy visits off-demonstration states.

ev-distribution-shift-imitation-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 15 describes learning a parameterized policy that represents a distribution over controls given states from demonstrations. This supports the page's discussion of the demonstration distribution and learned-policy behavior.
ev-distribution-shift-imitation-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page makes explicit the distribution-shift failure mode: a learned policy can visit states that the expert demonstrations did not cover.

ev-reward-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 16 contrasts directly learning a policy with learning the underlying objective or reward function optimized by the expert. This supports the reward page's role for reward as a behavioral objective signal.
ev-reward-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the reward-hacking boundary: a scalar reward may omit safety or task values and therefore incentivize unintended behavior.

ev-policy-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 16 says behavioral cloning can directly learn a policy that represents, mimics, and approximates expert behavior. This supports the policy page's definition of a policy as the action-selection rule.
ev-policy-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page generalizes from imitation to all control settings where a policy maps available state or observation information into actions.

ev-value-based-rl-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 17 introduces value-based methods as a category of model-free reinforcement-learning algorithms. This directly supports the value-based RL page.
ev-value-based-rl-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page explains the first-principles method role: learn future-return values and choose actions through those estimates.

ev-exploration-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 16 says the policy must explore the state and action space well enough for reinforcement-learning tools to be effective. This directly supports the exploration page.
ev-exploration-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page adds the control boundary that exploration must be balanced against safety, hardware limits, and data-collection cost.

ev-reachability-01.what_transcript_supports: Lecture 11 opens by continuing the reachability discussion and states that reachability theory computes reachable sets through the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation. It distinguishes avoidance sets and reach sets using target sets, disturbances, controls, and safety objectives.
ev-reachability-01.synthesis_beyond_transcript: The page turns that transcript passage into the learner-facing rule that reachability is set-valued reasoning about which states can still satisfy or avoid a target under the allowed dynamics, controls, and disturbances.
